lead: This unit turns diffusion into equipment numbers. You will calculate how fast a gas dissolves in a liquid, combine film resistances, use correlations and analogies, and size tray or packed contactors. After it you can estimate mass fluxes and the height or number of stages for absorption and similar operations.
about: This unit explains how fast mass crosses a phase boundary when the fluids are moving. Chapter 2.1 defines the convective mass transfer coefficient k_c. Chapter 2.2 combines gas-side and liquid-side coefficients into overall coefficients. Chapter 2.3 uses dimensionless groups to predict k_c from correlations. Chapters 2.4 and 2.5 explain the theories and the momentum–heat–mass analogies behind those correlations. Chapter 2.6 applies the two-resistance picture to interphase transfer. Chapters 2.7 and 2.8 count equilibrium stages and size tray and packed contactors. Chapter 2.9 adds chemical reaction in the film. After this unit you can calculate fluxes, convert between individual and overall coefficients, choose a correlation, and estimate the height or number of stages for a contactor.

chapters.idea: When a fluid moves past a surface, the mass flux is written with a convective coefficient k_c instead of a diffusion path length.
chapters.depth: Define k_c from N_A = k_c(C_Ai − C_A∞). Give its units m/s and the gas form k_G in kmol/(m²·s·atm) with a partial-pressure driving force. Distinguish local and average coefficients, gas-side and liquid-side values. Show how laminar flow over a plate gives a thin concentration boundary layer and a large gradient; turbulence and eddy diffusion raise k_c. Name the mass transfer coefficient concept and its types, as some syllabi phrase it.

figure.title: Convective flux path
figure.aria: A left-to-right block diagram from bulk gas through the gas film and interface into the liquid, with the two concentrations used in the worked example.

chapters.example: Air at 300 K and 1 atm flows over a water surface. The mass transfer coefficient is k_c = 0.02 m/s. The interface concentration of the transferred species in the gas is C_Ai = 0.50 mol/m³ and the bulk gas concentration is C_A∞ = 0.10 mol/m³. Find the molar flux N_A. Solution: N_A = k_c(C_Ai − C_A∞) = 0.02 × (0.50 − 0.10) = 0.008 mol/(m²·s).
chapters.trap: Using k_G with a concentration difference, or k_c with a partial-pressure difference, gives wrong units. Match the coefficient to its driving force.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: Fick's law and steady diffusion.
chapters.leave: Correlations to Chapter 2.3; theories to Chapter 2.4; absorber design to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Individual gas-film and liquid-film coefficients add as resistances to give one overall coefficient based on either phase.
chapters.depth: Write the two-film series relations 1/K_y = 1/k_y + m/k_x and 1/K_x = 1/(m k_y) + 1/k_x, where m is the slope of y* = m x. Define individual coefficients k_y, k_x and overall coefficients K_y, K_x. Compute the fraction of total resistance in each film and identify gas-film or liquid-film control. Use the same units and same driving-force basis in every term.

figure.title: Two resistances in series
figure.aria: A vertical block diagram of the gas film and liquid film in series between bulk gas and bulk liquid, with the resistance values from the worked example.

chapters.example: A gas is absorbed into a liquid. The individual coefficients are k_y = 0.05 kmol/(m²·s·Δy) and k_x = 0.08 kmol/(m²·s·Δx). The equilibrium line is y* = 1.5 x. Find K_y, K_x and the percentage of the gas-film resistance in K_y. Solution: 1/K_y = 1/0.05 + 1.5/0.08 = 20 + 18.75 = 38.75, so K_y = 0.0258 kmol/(m²·s·Δy). 1/K_x = 1/(1.5×0.05) + 1/0.08 = 13.33 + 12.50 = 25.83, so K_x = 0.0387 kmol/(m²·s·Δx). Gas-film share = 20/38.75 = 0.516, or 51.6%.
chapters.trap: Putting m on the wrong side of the resistance sum. For 1/K_y the liquid term is m/k_x; for 1/K_x the gas term is 1/(m k_y).
chapters.leave: Tower design and HTU/NTU to Unit 3 and Chapter 2.8.

chapters.idea: Dimensionless groups collapse many convective mass transfer experiments into correlations for the Sherwood number.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter in full. Define Sh = k_c L/D_AB, Re = ρuL/μ and Sc = μ/(ρD_AB), where L is length, u is velocity, ρ is density, μ is viscosity and D_AB is diffusivity. Give the flat-plate laminar correlation Sh = 0.664 Re^1/2 Sc^1/3, the flat-plate turbulent form Sh = 0.037 Re^0.8 Sc^1/3, and the sphere form Sh = 2 + 0.6 Re^1/2 Sc^1/3. Show how to choose L and evaluate properties. Mention that correlations are empirical fits to the same boundary-layer problem.

figure.aria: Two lines of Sherwood number against Reynolds number; the turbulent line rises more steeply, and the worked example point lies near the laminar line.

chapters.example: Air flows at u = 2 m/s over a flat plate of length L = 0.5 m. For the diffusing species, D_AB = 2.6×10⁻⁵ m²/s and ν = 1.5×10⁻⁵ m²/s. Use the laminar flat-plate correlation Sh = 0.664 Re^1/2 Sc^1/3. Find Re, Sc, Sh and k_c. Solution: Re = uL/ν = 2×0.5/(1.5×10⁻⁵) = 6.67×10⁴. Sc = ν/D_AB = 1.5/2.6 = 0.577. Sh = 0.664 × √(6.67×10⁴) × (0.577)^(1/3) = 0.664 × 258.3 × 0.833 = 142.8. k_c = Sh D_AB/L = 142.8 × 2.6×10⁻⁵ / 0.5 = 7.4×10⁻³ m/s.
chapters.trap: Using a correlation with a different length scale or with properties at the wrong temperature. Use the same L as the correlation defines and evaluate at film temperature.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 and fluid mechanics: Reynolds number and boundary layers.
chapters.leave: Full boundary-layer derivation; only the three correlations are used here.

chapters.idea: Film, penetration and surface-renewal theories give different ways to interpret k_c in terms of a film thickness or exposure time.
chapters.depth: Present film theory k_c = D/δ, penetration theory k_c = 2√(D/(πt)), and surface renewal theory k_c = √(D s). Define δ (equivalent film thickness), t (exposure time) and s (fractional surface renewal rate). Compare the predicted dependence on D: film gives k_c ∝ D, the other two give k_c ∝ √D. Explain why eddy diffusion near the interface makes the simple film picture approximate.

figure.aria: A stack of three mass transfer theories with their predicted coefficients; film theory gives the smallest value and penetration theory the largest in the worked example.

chapters.example: For a sparingly soluble gas, D = 2×10⁻⁹ m²/s and k_L = 1.0×10⁻⁵ m/s from a film model with δ = 0.2 mm. Find the film thickness prediction, the penetration prediction for t = 0.5 s, and the surface-renewal prediction for s = 2 s⁻¹. Solution: film k_L = D/δ = 2×10⁻⁹ / 2×10⁻⁴ = 1.0×10⁻⁵ m/s. Penetration k_L = 2√(D/(πt)) = 2√(2×10⁻⁹/(π×0.5)) = 7.1×10⁻⁵ m/s. Surface renewal k_L = √(D s) = √(2×10⁻⁹×2) = 6.3×10⁻⁵ m/s.
chapters.trap: Treating δ as a real measured film thickness. It is an equivalent thickness chosen to match k_c; the penetration and surface-renewal models fit many liquid systems better.
chapters.leave: Detailed turbulence modelling; analogy derivations to Chapter 2.5.

chapters.idea: Momentum, heat and mass transfer share the same eddy diffusivity, so one friction factor can predict k_c.
chapters.depth: State the Reynolds analogy St = f/2 for Pr = 1, and the Chilton-Colburn form j_H = j_D = f/2, with j_D = Sh/(Re Sc^1/3) and j_H = Nu/(Re Pr^1/3). Define f (Fanning friction factor), St (Stanton number), Nu (Nusselt number) and Pr (Prandtl number). Mention Prandtl-Taylor and von Kármán as refinements. Use the analogy to estimate k_c from a measured pressure drop.

figure.title: Chilton-Colburn analogy
figure.aria: A three-block diagram linking momentum, heat and mass transfer through the same eddy diffusivity and the Chilton-Colburn equality.

chapters.example: Air flows over a smooth flat plate. The Fanning friction factor is f = 0.008. Estimate j_D, Sh and k_c for Re = 5×10⁴, Sc = 0.6, D_AB = 2.5×10⁻⁵ m²/s and L = 0.5 m. Solution: j_D = f/2 = 0.004. Sc^(1/3) = 0.843. Sh = j_D Re Sc^(1/3) = 0.004×5×10⁴×0.843 = 168.6. k_c = Sh D_AB/L = 168.6×2.5×10⁻⁵/0.5 = 8.4×10⁻³ m/s.
chapters.trap: Applying j_D = j_H = f/2 when form drag or high mass-transfer rates are present. The analogy holds for smooth walls and small transfer rates.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.3 and basic fluid mechanics and heat transfer.

chapters.idea: At the interface the two phases are in equilibrium, and the two film resistances fix the interface composition and flux.
chapters.depth: State the two-resistance assumptions: equilibrium at the interface, no accumulation, and equal fluxes through both films. Show how to find interface compositions from k_y(y − y_i) = k_x(x_i − x) and y_i = m x_i. Define overall driving forces y − y* and x* − x. Use resistance ratios to decide whether the gas film or the liquid film controls. Give one example each: ammonia in water is gas-film controlled, oxygen in water is liquid-film controlled.

figure.aria: A plot of the equilibrium line y = 2x, the bulk point (0.02, 0.10), and the interface point (0.0367, 0.0733) on the line.

chapters.example: In an absorption column, bulk gas y = 0.10 and bulk liquid x = 0.02 (mole fractions). The equilibrium line is y* = 2x. The individual coefficients are k_y = 0.05 kmol/(m²·s·Δy) and k_x = 0.08 kmol/(m²·s·Δx). Find the interface compositions and the flux. Solution: set k_y(y − y_i) = k_x(x_i − x) and y_i = 2x_i. 0.05(0.10 − 2x_i) = 0.08(x_i − 0.02). This gives 0.005 − 0.10x_i = 0.08x_i − 0.0016, so x_i = 0.0367 and y_i = 0.0733. N_A = 0.05(0.10 − 0.0733) = 1.33×10⁻³ kmol/(m²·s).
chapters.trap: Assuming the bulk phases are in equilibrium. Equilibrium holds only at the interface; the bulk driving force is y − y* with y* in equilibrium with the bulk liquid.
chapters.leave: Absorption column design to Unit 3; extraction to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: An ideal stage leaves its exiting streams in equilibrium; a real stage needs an efficiency to convert ideal stages into actual trays.
chapters.depth: Define an ideal equilibrium stage: exiting liquid and vapor are in equilibrium. Write the Murphree vapor efficiency E_M = (y_n − y_{n+1})/(y_n* − y_{n+1}) and the overall efficiency E_o = N_ideal/N_actual. Explain cross-current and counter-current cascades and how an operating line steps between stages. Introduce the Kremser equation for a fixed number of stages. Distinguish stage efficiency from the equilibrium-stage count.

figure.title: Murphree efficiency
figure.aria: A down block diagram of vapor entering stage n, leaving at y_n = 0.16, and the equilibrium value y_n* = 0.20 used in the Murphree efficiency.

chapters.example: On a tray, the vapor entering from below has y_{n+1} = 0.10 and the vapor leaving has y_n = 0.16. The vapor leaving would be in equilibrium with the liquid leaving at y_n* = 0.20. Find the Murphree vapor efficiency. If the ideal stage count is 10 and the overall efficiency is 0.60, find the actual stage count. Solution: E_M = (0.16 − 0.10)/(0.20 − 0.10) = 0.60. N_actual = N_ideal/E_o = 10/0.60 = 16.7, so 17 stages.
chapters.trap: Using the equilibrium value with the entering liquid or vapor instead of the leaving stream. Murphree efficiency uses y_n* in equilibrium with the liquid leaving the tray.
chapters.leave: McCabe-Thiele and reflux to Unit 4; detailed Kremser design to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Tray contactors are counted as stages, while packed contactors are sized by the product of HTU and NTU.
chapters.depth: Compare stage-wise contactors (trays, mixers) with differential contactors (packed towers). For trays use HETP = Z/N_actual and stage efficiency. For packed towers write Z = HTU × NTU, with HTU = G/K_y a and NTU = ∫ dy/(y* − y) between the terminal compositions. Define G (molar gas flux), K_y a (volumetric overall coefficient) and y* (equilibrium mole fraction). Show that both methods answer the same design question: how much contactor height is needed.

figure.title: Stage or packed height
figure.aria: A block diagram splitting contactor choice into tray stages and packed differential contact, then showing HETP for trays and Z = HTU × NTU for packing.

chapters.example: A packed absorber has a gas molar flux G = 0.02 kmol/(m²·s) and a volumetric overall coefficient K_y a = 0.05 kmol/(m³·s·Δy). The required NTU is 3.5. Find HTU and packed height Z. Solution: HTU = G/(K_y a) = 0.02/0.05 = 0.4 m. Z = HTU × NTU = 0.4×3.5 = 1.4 m.
chapters.trap: Mixing up HETP and HTU. HETP is height per ideal stage; HTU is height per transfer unit, and Z = HTU×NTU.
chapters.leave: Absorber and stripper design to Unit 3; distillation column design to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A chemical reaction in the liquid film steepens the concentration gradient and raises the mass flux by an enhancement factor.
chapters.depth: Add a reaction in the liquid film. Define the Hatta number Ha = √(k D)/k_L for first-order reaction and the enhancement factor E = k_L(with reaction)/k_L(no reaction). Describe slow (E ≈ 1), fast (E ≈ Ha) and instantaneous (E limited by both reactants) regimes. Apply to reactive absorption such as CO2 in amine or H2S in alkali. Keep reaction kinetics brief; the focus is the effect on the flux.

figure.aria: Concentration profiles in the film for no reaction, slow reaction and fast reaction; reaction steepens the gradient near the interface.

chapters.example: A first-order reaction with k = 10 s⁻¹ occurs in the liquid film. D = 2×10⁻⁹ m²/s and k_L = 1.0×10⁻⁵ m/s without reaction. Find the Hatta number and the enhancement factor for the fast-reaction regime. Solution: Ha = √(kD)/k_L = √(10×2×10⁻⁹)/(1.0×10⁻⁵) = 1.41×10⁻⁴/1.0×10⁻⁵ = 14.1. For fast pseudo-first-order reaction E ≈ Ha = 14.1. The flux is about 14 times the non-reacting flux.
chapters.trap: Using Ha = √(kD)/k_L with the gas-side k. For absorption with reaction, use the liquid-side k_L and liquid diffusivity.
chapters.leave: Reactive absorption equipment design to Unit 3; specific chemical systems.

links: correlations and analogies both predict k_c
